problem: Existing household-safety benchmarks either abstract scenes into text (losing visual cues) or fix the viewpoint / prescribe tasks, so none tests whether an embodied agent can actively explore a home and discover an unknown set of hazards from egocentric views.
motivation: Home hazards (flammables near stoves, sharp tools within a child's reach) cause preventable injuries, and an automated inspector needs active exploration under partial observability. Evaluating VLMs this way shows a large gap to humans, with precision far above recall, so the models under-report hazards, which points to a shared deficiency in risk recognition. Online RL in the heavy Unity simulator is too costly, so a cheap offline recipe is needed.
key_idea: Build a free-exploration home safety inspection benchmark (HomeSafeBench), and train small VLMs with CueBack, which backtracks privileged trajectories to the earliest frame where a hazard cue becomes visible and rewrites the reasoning as exploration before the cue and confirmation after it.
insight: Most of the gain comes from the simulator-free executable trajectories: SFT-Action alone (37.8 F1) already beats the best closed-source model (34.7). The clue-aware reasoning adds a further gain over naive GPT-5.5 rationales (SFT-Both 39.3 -> CueBack 45.3), presumably because it avoids leaking privileged hazard knowledge into exploration steps. Behavior analysis shows untrained VLMs report as often as trained ones but explore little (GPT-5.5 spends 58% of actions turning in place), so the bottleneck is recognition and coverage, not reluctance to report. Action ablations show free exploration matters: w/o walk costs CueBack 16.1 F1, while GPT-5.5 loses only 2.4, so it barely exploits exploration.
method: Benchmark construction: 12 VirtualHome rooms annotated by humans with 136 hazard locations and 367 objects with safety attributes; rule-based pairing gives 3,042 single-hazard candidates; GPT-filtering on 10 rendered views keeps 580; these are composed into 1,000 test tasks with 1-5 hazards each (3,000 hazard instances).

Agent/task interface: the agent gets 640x360 egocentric views and calls one tool per step (walk 1-5 steps, turn 30-180°, look_up/look_down, report_hazard, finish_inspection) within a 20-step budget; evaluation uses category-level and hazard-level (GPT-5.5 judge, one-to-one matching) P/R/F1.

Room-level observation graph and trajectory synthesis: humans annotate nodes (inspection viewpoints with coverage sets) and directed navigation edges; routes covering all target hazards are ranked by cost, replayed in the simulator and validated (within 1 m of each node, target >=50 px in the segmentation), giving 3,158 executable trajectories from 3,400 training tasks.

Clue-precedes-confirmation boundary localization: GPT-5.5 finds, for each report segment, the earliest navigation step where the hazard or its risk area becomes visible; earlier steps are labeled free_explore, later ones approach_inspect, plus report and finish.

Stage-aware reasoning generation: GPT-5.5 writes short reasoning (<=45 words) for each fixed action conditioned on the stage label (exploration style without naming unseen hazards, confirmation style referencing visible clues), inserted before the tool call.
Training: LoRA (r=16, alpha=32) SFT of Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking for 1 epoch, lr 1e-4, with the vision encoder frozen; train environments, scenes and objects are disjoint from the test set.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking (LoRA fine-tuned) for CueBack; evaluated baselines are Seed-2.0-Pro, GPT-5.5, GLM-5V-Turbo, Qwen-3.6-Plus, Kimi-K2.5 and Qwen3-VL-8B/4B/30B-A3B-Thinking (frozen)
setting.training_data: 3,158 simulator-replayed executable trajectories from 3,400 VirtualHome training tasks (2 environments, 8 rooms) with GPT-5.5-generated clue-aware reasoning
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB (640x360) with full interaction history
setting.action_space: semantic tool calls: walk (1-5 steps), turn (30°-180° in 30° steps), look_up/look_down (5-75°), report_hazard, finish_inspection; max 20 steps
setting.privileged: none at test time; privileged room graph and hazard locations are used only for offline training-data trajectory synthesis

results: The best off-the-shelf VLM, Seed-2.0-Pro, reaches only 34.7 F1 against 98.0 for a human, with precision far above recall across models. CueBack raises Qwen3-VL-4B from 18.7 to 45.3 F1, beating SFT-Both (39.3), DPO (29.1) and the best closed-source model (34.7) on the out-of-distribution test set.
limitations: Restricted to the simulated VirtualHome (few rooms, rule-generated hazards from templates), with no real-world validation.
Data generation and hazard judging both depend on GPT-5.5, and the test set is small in scene diversity (one held-out environment, 4 rooms).
Even the best model is at 45.3 F1 vs 98 for humans; recall on falling-object and child-safety hazards stays low.
